The vector $\mathbf{v}_{c'}$ affects a single score, so the sum collapses to the term $k = c'$. The vector $\mathbf{e}_w$ affects every score, so all the terms survive, and the delta keeps only $k = c$ in the second part:
$$
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \mathbf{v}_{c'}} = \bigl(Q(c' \mid w) - \delta_{c'c}\bigr)\,\mathbf{e}_w, \qquad
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \mathbf{e}_w} = \sum_{k} \bigl(Q(k \mid w) - \delta_{kc}\bigr)\,\mathbf{v}_k = -\mathbf{v}_c + \sum_{k} Q(k \mid w)\,\mathbf{v}_k.
$$
5. A gradient descent step with learning rate $\eta$ moves every vector against its gradient:
$$
\mathbf{e}_w \leftarrow \mathbf{e}_w + \eta\Bigl(\mathbf{v}_c - \sum_{k} Q(k \mid w)\,\mathbf{v}_k\Bigr), \qquad
\mathbf{v}_{c'} \leftarrow \mathbf{v}_{c'} - \eta\,\bigl(Q(c' \mid w) - \delta_{c'c}\bigr)\,\mathbf{e}_w \quad \text{for every } c' \in V.
$$

The derivatives with respect to all the scores add up to $1 - 1 = 0$, as they must, because adding a constant to every score leaves $Q$ unchanged (and properly normalized). Gradient descent then raises the score of the observed neighbour in proportion to the probability that the model failed to give it, and lowers the scores of the others in proportion to the probability that the model gave them.
:::

Given the cross-entropy as the loss function, let's try to reproduce the previous section's results on the toy corpus of thriteen phrases describing a sky and a court with queens and kings.

TODO: show results equivalent tables of results that @tbl-svd and @tbl-patterns

If counting and predicting reach the same object, why did prediction win? In 2015 Levy, Goldberg and Dagan took the design choices that came with word2vec and transferred them to PPMI and SVD [@levy2015improving]. Much of the gap closed. They observed "mostly local or insignificant performance differences between the methods, with no global advantage to any single approach" [@levy2015improving, p. 211]. What prediction bought was not a better geometry. It was an algorithm that uses computation in the way Sutton's bitter lesson describes: memory proportional to the vocabulary rather than to its square, a cost per step independent of the corpus, steps that run in parallel on many processors, and vectors that keep improving as more text is read. This is the first concrete form of the bitter lesson in this book, and it concerns the algorithm, not the shape of the model, which is the same low-rank factorization as before, as linear as an SVD.

Prediction has a second advantage that counting lacks, since its objective never mentions a matrix. It says only "predict a neighbour from a word", and nothing prevents the word from becoming something richer. Predict the next word from all the words before it, replace the lookup of $\mathbf{e}_w$ by a network that reads the whole context, and keep the cross-entropy. That is how large language models are trained, and their last layer is a softmax over the scores $\langle \mathbf{h}, \mathbf{v}_c \rangle$, the expression of $Q(c \mid w)$ with a vector $\mathbf{h}$ computed from the context in place of $\mathbf{e}_w$. Chapter 4 takes up these contextual vectors. They also repair a cost shared by every method of this chapter, that of having one vector per word. The `bank` of a river and the `bank` that lends money share a single row of $\mathbf{E}$, a compromise between the two uses weighted by their frequency, and only a vector computed from the sentence can tell them apart.

Look once more at the gradient of the predictor. Each step pulls the word towards the neighbour that the text shows and pushes it away from all the others, so learning to predict is learning to pick the right neighbour out of a list of candidates. Seen this way, the word, its window and even the vocabulary were never essential. All the method needs is a source of pairs that belong together and a set of alternatives to tell them from, and both can come from anywhere: two programs that agree on the same probe inputs, a photograph and its caption, the frames and the sound of one video. The next section replaces the vocabulary by a batch of such alternatives, drops the word and keeps the contrast.

::: {.questions}
1. Fix a word $w$ and let $p_c = P(c \mid w)$ be the true probability of each neighbour $c$, and $q_c = Q(c \mid w)$ the probability given by a softmax predictor. The cross-entropy for this word is $-\sum_c p_c \ln q_c$. Using the inequality $\ln t \le t - 1$, show that $-\sum_c p_c \ln q_c \ge -\sum_c p_c \ln p_c$, with equality only when $q_c = p_c$ for every $c$, so the best predictor reproduces the true conditional probabilities. Then find all the scores $x_{wc}$ for which the softmax gives $q_c = p_c$, and write them in terms of $\mathrm{PMI}(w,c)$ and $P(c)$. Why are the scores of a word fixed only up to a constant that is added to all of them? What does the score of a pair that never occurs have to be?

2. Download a book as plain text from the Internet (for example, from Project Gutenberg), split its words into the first 90% for training and the last 10% for testing, and let $V$ be the vocabulary of the whole book. Compute the cross-entropy of the test text, in bits per word, under two predictors estimated on the training part: a unigram model, $Q(c) = (C_c + 1)/(T + |V|)$, where $C_c$ is the count of $c$ and $T$ the number of training words, and a bigram model, $Q(c \mid w) = (C_{wc} + 1)/(C_w + |V|)$, where $C_{wc}$ counts $c$ right after $w$. Which predictor compresses the test text better? What fraction of the consecutive word pairs of the test text never occurs in the training text? Explain the result, and say why a predictor computed from word vectors, as in this section, could do better than both.

3. Using PyTorch, train the softmax predictor on the co-occurrence counts of the thirteen sentences of Counting Company (window of one word), for $d = 2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 12$ and five random seeds each. Instead of sampling windows, minimize the cross-entropy summed over all the pairs, $-\sum_{w,c} C_{wc} \ln Q(c \mid w)$, with Adam (learning rate 0.01, 30,000 steps), starting from small random vectors. Build the learned counterpart of @tbl-svd, the cosines of the same five pairs of rows of $\mathbf{E}$ for each $d$ (mean and range over the seeds), with the final loss per pair and $\ln Q(\texttt{king} \mid \texttt{dawn})$ next to them, and print the rows of $\mathbf{E}$ for $d = 5$ as @tbl-patterns did for the SVD. Compare the final loss with the conditional entropy $H(C \mid W)$ of the corpus, and $Q(\texttt{breaks} \mid \texttt{dawn})$ and $Q(\texttt{the} \mid \texttt{dawn})$ with the true probabilities. Finally, for $d = 5$, multiply $\mathbf{E}$ by $\mathrm{diag}(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)$ and $\mathbf{V}$ by its inverse, and see what happens to the loss and to the cosines. You now have two sets of tables for the same corpus, one from the SVD and one from gradient descent. What is going on? Which numbers agree with the SVD and which do not, which are the same in every run and which change, and why? What does $d$ do now, and how would you choose it?
:::

## Learning by Contrast

*Plan (3 pages).* InfoNCE, a softmax over a batch of candidates instead of the vocabulary, descended from noise-contrastive estimation [@gutmann2010noise]: pull positive pairs together and push negatives apart, a lower bound on mutual information, Shannon's third quantity. The temperature $\tau$ as the dial between easy and hard negatives. Wang and Isola's decomposition into alignment and uniformity on the hypersphere [@wang2020understanding]. Connect back to the behavioural embedding of programs in the Rice exercises: two programs that agree on the probes are a positive pair. The pattern is contrastive learning with negatives, and InfoNCE is the instance that made it standard; CLIP is one dated application, not the lesson. Nothing in the objective requires the two members of a positive pair to be of the same kind: an image and its caption, or the frames and the audio track of one video, are positive pairs too, and Chapter 12 builds on this. The bitter lesson again: no one writes the similarity table, because the data supplies the positive pairs and the batch supplies the negatives, so the method improves as data and compute grow. This is the objective behind the sentence embeddings used for retrieval in Chapter 3. Exercise: contrastive training of program or sentence embeddings on a toy set.

## Learning by Predicting Embeddings

*Plan (2–3 pages).* A fourth objective, which keeps prediction but changes its target. Learning by Prediction predicts the neighbour itself, and pays in bits for every detail of it; Learning by Contrast picks the neighbour out of a batch of negatives. A joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) predicts the *embedding* of a missing part from the embedding of its context: two encoders, one for the context and one for the target, and a predictor between them, with the loss measured as a distance in the embedding space rather than as a surprisal over the vocabulary. What cannot be predicted from the context need not be represented, so the vector keeps what context and target share, much as in Learning by Contrast though without its bound on mutual information, and without a softmax over the vocabulary or negatives. data2vec (2022) applies the idea to text, speech, and images alike, predicting at masked positions the averaged inner-layer vectors of a target network [@baevski2022data2vec]; the image and video forms named JEPA are told in Chapter 12.

The price of dropping negatives is collapse. If every input is mapped to the same vector, the prediction is perfect and the space says nothing; a milder failure, dimensional collapse, uses only a few of the $d$ directions. Negatives were what kept the space spread out, Wang and Isola's uniformity [@wang2020understanding], so something else must do it. Two answers, told as history: an asymmetric design in which the target encoder is a slowly moving average of the context encoder (BYOL, 2020) [@grill2020bootstrap], and explicit terms that keep the variance of every coordinate up and their covariances down (VICReg, 2022) [@bardes2022vicreg], the second a close cousin of the uniformity that negatives used to supply.

- Claim: the four objectives are four ways of making a vector keep what the company of a signal predicts. Prediction pays in bits for every detail of the company, and counting pays in reconstruction error on the PMI matrix of all of it; contrast and latent prediction pay only for what distinguishes it, and differ in what keeps the space from collapsing.
- Bitter lesson: latent prediction is argued for as the general method for signals too rich to predict in detail [@lecun2022path], and against it as a prior that scaled generative models absorb; the question is left to the scale test of Chapter 12.
- Hooks: collapse as the extreme of the anisotropy of Where a Single Vector Strains and of the directions of Chapter 2; prediction in latent space and world models in Chapter 12; predictive processing in the Epilogue.
- Exercise: train a toy latent predictor on the corpus of this chapter, watch it collapse, measure the effective rank of the embeddings, and restore it with a moving-average target or a variance term.

## The Geometry of Meaning

*Plan (3–4 pages).* On the unit sphere cosine similarity and Euclidean distance carry the same information, $\|\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}\|_2^2 = 2 - 2\cos\theta$; the direction of a vector encodes its category and its norm encodes frequency and salience. Mikolov's analogy parallelogram, $\mathbf{v}_{\text{king}} - \mathbf{v}_{\text{man}} + \mathbf{v}_{\text{woman}} \approx \mathbf{v}_{\text{queen}}$ [@mikolov2013efficient], and why it follows from ratios of co-occurrence probabilities becoming differences of logarithms [@arora2016latent; @pennington2014glove]. This is where GloVe belongs: it fits the vectors by a weighted least squares on the logarithms of the non-zero counts, $\sum f(C_{wc})(\langle \mathbf{e}_w, \mathbf{v}_c\rangle + b_w + \tilde b_c - \ln C_{wc})^2$, so the dot product is again a PMI, and its derivation starts from those ratios. A brief note on steering vectors: the same linear structure, found inside the activations of modern LLMs, and developed in Chapter 4 as the linear representation hypothesis. Keep three claims apart: that dot products are what hardware computes cheaply (why linear read-outs scale), that concepts are directions in learned spaces (an empirical claim about what training finds), and the bitter lesson (a claim about methods, which does not say that the winner is linear). Exercise: test analogies on pre-trained vectors and find where they fail.

## Where a Single Vector Strains

*Plan (2–3 pages).* Anisotropy: trained embeddings crowd into a narrow cone, so that all cosines are high, and the simple remedies of centring and whitening. Hubness, a few points that are the nearest neighbour of almost everything, as a first sign of the strangeness of high dimensions studied in Chapter 2. Close with, in prose, the ledger of limits that the rest of the book examines. Each is stated as a cost, not as an impossibility, and each says whether it is structural or contingent: a nearest-neighbour query cannot negate or chain, and a fixed-dimension dot product can realize only a limited family of rankings (Chapter 3); flat space needs more dimensions than curved space to hold a hierarchy at the same distortion (Chapter 5); symmetric dot products cannot express asymmetric relations (Chapter 6); pairwise structure does not directly encode multi-way interactions (Chapter 7); similarity alone is not a logic, because negation and conjunction need more than a score (Chapter 8); a sum of vectors cannot say which attribute belongs to which object, the binding problem (Chapter 9); systematic composition is the open question of Chapter 10; the coordinates of a trained space are arbitrary up to an isometry, so comparing two spaces is a problem of its own (Chapter 11); and a space shared across senses keeps only what its views have in common, while embeddings of different modalities remain in separate cones, the modality gap (Chapter 12). End on the other side of the ledger: the thesis is not that a single vector fails and a richer geometry repairs it, but that a single vector is a strong first answer and every extension is a trade. For each limit the question is whether more dimensions, data and compute substitute for the added structure, which is the bitter lesson applied to geometry.

{{< pagebreak >}}

## Further Reading {.unnumbered}

Counting, predicting and contrasting are not unrelated techniques but convergent estimators of the same co-occurrence statistics. @arora2016latent develops the latent-variable argument for why PMI-based factorization and log-bilinear regression agree, and @pennington2014glove derives the GloVe objective in full. @sutton2019bitter is a short statement of the pattern that this chapter traces from counting to predicting to contrasting. For the PCA and SVD material of "From Counting to Geometry", @hastie2009elements (Section 14.5) is a standard textbook treatment, and @eckart1936approximation is the original proof that truncating the SVD gives the best low-rank approximation. The next chapter's argument about embedding dimensionality rests on the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma [@johnson1984extensions, pp. 189-206], which bounds how much a point set can be projected into lower dimensions while approximately preserving pairwise distances.
